On Wednesday, March 21, 2012 2:22:03 PM UTC+3, Finn Lindgren wrote:
>
> On Wednesday, 21 March 2012 11:08:35 UTC+1, Laura Serra Saurina wrote:
> > I would like to know the difference between the two types of zero-inflated models (type 0 and type 1). Looking at the formula I noticed that type 0 only includes positives values and type 1 includes all kind of values. Is there any other difference?
> >
> > Type 0: Prob(y|...) = p x 1[y=0] + (1 - p) x Poisson(y | y > 0)
> >
> > Type 1: Prob(y|...) = p x 1[y=0] + (1 - p) x Poisson(y)
> Type 1 is a mixture of a point mass at 0 and a regular Poisson distribution, whereas Type 0 is a mixture of a truncated Poisson (the y>0 bit) and a point mass at 0, so that the probability at zero is governed directly by p.
>
> This means e.g. that Type 0 can have a _lower_ probability at 0 than a pure Poisson, relative to the probability at 1, whereas Type 1 can only increase the relative probability for 0.
>
> >
> > Moreover, could you give me the Type2's formula? I haven't found it.
> The description of Type 2 is at the end of page 6 of
> http://www.math.ntnu.no/~hrue/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/zeroinflated.pdf <http://www.math.ntnu.no/%7Ehrue/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/zeroinflated.pdf>
> It's like Type 1 but with a different definition of p.
>
> /Finn
>

 I am new to INLA and i was trying to fit a zero inflated poisson model (0) but i required the model to include a spatial component for example CAR model

i seem to be fitting the model well without fail when i do not include the spatial component, but perhaps am missing some part of model specification or parameters

my data distribution has a classical zero-inflated like histogram with very few large values

my question is 1) is a specification of spatial component the right thing to do e.g using besag 2) how best do i initiate the parameters when i call INLA

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Zero-inflated models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Victor,
Without being able to try it on your dataset, it's hard to know
exactly what happened.

I ran the following code, where the graph and data were taken from the
bym example.

library(INLA)

#taken from BYM example. Read data and graph and organise dataframe
data(Germany)
g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))
Germany = cbind(Germany,region.struct=Germany$region)

#this is similar to your formula
formula1 = Y ~ f(region.struct,model="besag",graph.file=g) +x

#this is similar to your inla call
result = inla(formula1, family="zeroinflatedpoisson0",data=Germany,
E=E, control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE))

summary(result)

I get sensible results, but the following warning message is produced:
"Warning message:
In INLA::f(region.struct, model = "besag", graph.file = g) :
  Argument 'graph.file' in 'f()' is obsolete; please use the more
general argument 'graph' instead."

You can get rid of this by changing the formula to
formula1 = Y ~ f(region.struct,model="besag",graph=g) +x

So, can you please send me the exact error message that you got when
you tried to run the problem.  There are also some things that you can
check:
-- Is INLA updated? Use inla.update(testing=TRUE)
-- Is your graph file valid?  Use inla.debug.graph()
-- Is the data frame in order?

Best wishes,

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA Team,
I am interested in fitting birth-death models using INLA.
I wanted to know whether it may be possible to have some guidance on how to get started. In my application I have counts on the terminal nodes of a phylogenetic tree. I want to fit the data into a BD model an estimate the birth and dead rates. I am interested in a couple of questions: a) whether groups of branches on the tree differ on their parameter values, and b) estimating the parameters for each branch on the tree. This model is of the kind described on "Streamlining and Large Ancestral Genomes in Archaea Inferred with a Phylogenetic Birth-and-Death Model".
Let me know if you think this may be possible and I can put together some examples files if you need them to construct and some example code.

Best and thanks in advance,
Inti Pedroso

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prior for Poisson
messages.body_plain:
In this case lambda is connected to the linear predictor through

log(lambda) = eta

What you could do is to define the linear predictor as a intercept and use the default Normal distribution for the intercept. I mean, use

formula = y ~ 1

and change the prior mean and precision for the intercept with control.fixed. Just to mention this model you described is quite simple and even has closed form solution, see for ex. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution#Bayesian_inference.

Best,
Thiago

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Simulation of Intrinsic CAR process
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karim,
The problem with simulating an intrinisic CAR model is that it is
intrinsic and, therefore, improper.  Therefore, it only makes sense to
simulate conditional on some constraints (such as a sum to zero
constraint).

So, I guess  the first and most important question is: are you sure
you really want to do this!  Have you considered using a proper model?
 (also note - that the limiting GRF is also improper, being a Matern
field with kappa=0, and simulating from it is also non-trivial!)

The theoretical way of doing this is to compute the eigendecomposition
of the precision matrix (i.e. compute eigenpairs (lambda_i, e_i) ),
and do the following

Set x=0
For every non-zero lambda_i
  Simulate y ~ N(0, lambda_i^{-1})
  x = x + y*e_i
End For

If you are on a regular grid, you can use a FFT to compute the
eigendecomposition (see Håvard's book on GMRFs).

Of course, you often don't have an eigendecomposition! Another option,
if R [or matlab] will let you compute a Cholesky factorisation of an
positive semi-definite matrix, is compute the Cholesky decomposition Q
= L L^T, then the least-squares solution to L^Tx=z, where z is a
vector of i.i.d. standard normals will be a sample.

Another option is to let F be a matrix with columns that make a basis
for the nullspace of Q (i.e. QF =0).  Then, sample from the proper
GMRF with precision Q + FF^T conditionally on F^Tx = 0.

If you want to go completely crazy, it's fairly straightforward to do
with Krylov Subspace methods, however, I probably wouldn't recommend
this route!  It's a bit fiddly and, I suspect, more "expert
level"/"experimental" than you're looking for.

It possible that Håvard has a clever method that I haven't thought of,
but when it comes down to it, this is a slightly odd problem that I
don't think there is an elegant, efficient numerical solution to the
problem.

Hope this helps,
Dan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Simulation of Intrinsic CAR process
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karim,
This is a tricky question.  In the end it depends on how the variance
parameter goes to zero.  If the model is on a regular lattice and the
space between points is h, then, if the variance goes to zero like
h^2, then this limits towards a de Wijs field.  If it goes to zero
faster than that, then it will shrink to zero (or, more specifically,
it will shrink to a de Wijs field with zero variance, which is an odd
thing).  If it goes to zero slower, it will not converge to a limit.

Other than slightly insane "counter examples", I can't think of a GMRF
that limits to an i.i.d. process (i.e. white noise) that isn't the
same as having independent Gaussians on each component.  In fact, I'm
pretty sure that "eventually", all GMRFs that limit to white noise
have to have this form.

Similarly, I'm struggling to come up with something that limits to a constant.

I hope this helps

Dan

yes! using this trick.

1. make the linear predictor equals each one of the component of the
model. so eta[1] = intercept, eta[2] = x1[1], eta[3] = x1[2], etc..,

2. build the model using the A-matrix.

here is your example; I think I got it correct.

******************

n = 3
m = 6
x1 = rnorm(m,mean=0,sd=1)
x2 = rnorm(n,mean=0,sd=1)
A = matrix(c(rep(1,6),c(1,0,1,0,1,0),c(0,1,0,1,0,1)),nrow=m,ncol=n)
y = 1+x1+A%*%x2

N = n + m + 1
intercept = c(1, rep(NA, N-1))
xx1 = c(NA, 1:m, rep(NA, N-(m+1)))
xx2 = c(NA, rep(NA, m), 1:n)

formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(xx1, model="iid") + f(xx2, model="iid")
AA = matrix(0, m, N)

AA[, 1] = 1
for(i in 1:m) {
    AA[i, 1+i] = 1
}

for(i in 1:n) {
    AA[, N-n+i] = A[, i]
}

r = inla(formula, data = list(y=y, xx1=xx1, xx2=xx2),
        control.predictor = list(A=AA))

> >  the to use a process that either degenerates to a constant (0) or converges
> > to an iid process
> > How can I do that?
> >
> > Thanks
> >
> > Karim
> >
> >
> > On Friday, May 18, 2012 11:57:12 AM UTC+1, Daniel Simpson wrote:
> >>
> >> Hi Karim,
> >> The problem with simulating an intrinisic CAR model is that it is
> >> intrinsic and, therefore, improper.  Therefore, it only makes sense to
> >> simulate conditional on some constraints (such as a sum to zero
> >> constraint).
> >>
> >> So, I guess  the first and most important question is: are you sure
> >> you really want to do this!  Have you considered using a proper model?
> >>  (also note - that the limiting GRF is also improper, being a Matern
> >> field with kappa=0, and simulating from it is also non-trivial!)
> >>
> >>
> >> The theoretical way of doing this is to compute the eigendecomposition
> >> of the precision matrix (i.e. compute eigenpairs (lambda_i, e_i) ),
> >> and do the following
> >>
> >> Set x=0
> >> For every non-zero lambda_i
> >>   Simulate y ~ N(0, lambda_i^{-1})
> >>   x = x + y*e_i
> >> End For
> >>
> >> If you are on a regular grid, you can use a FFT to compute the
> >> eigendecomposition (see Håvard's book on GMRFs).
> >>
> >> Of course, you often don't have an eigendecomposition! Another option,
> >> if R [or matlab] will let you compute a Cholesky factorisation of an
> >> positive semi-definite matrix, is compute the Cholesky decomposition Q
> >> = L L^T, then the least-squares solution to L^Tx=z, where z is a
> >> vector of i.i.d. standard normals will be a sample.
> >>
> >> Another option is to let F be a matrix with columns that make a basis
> >> for the nullspace of Q (i.e. QF =0).  Then, sample from the proper
> >> GMRF with precision Q + FF^T conditionally on F^Tx = 0.
> >>
> >> If you want to go completely crazy, it's fairly straightforward to do
> >> with Krylov Subspace methods, however, I probably wouldn't recommend
> >> this route!  It's a bit fiddly and, I suspect, more "expert
> >> level"/"experimental" than you're looking for.
> >>
> >> It possible that Håvard has a clever method that I haven't thought of,
> >> but when it comes down to it, this is a slightly odd problem that I
> >> don't think there is an elegant, efficient numerical solution to the
> >> problem.
> >>
> >> Hope this helps,
> >> Dan
> >>
> >> On 18 May 2012 11:06, Karim Anaya  wrote:
> >> > Hi there
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > I am interested in simulating an intrinsic CAR process over a specific
> >> > lattice (map).
> >> > Does the INLA package can help on this? otherwise any advice (reference)
> >> > on
> >> > how to do this efficiently.
> >> > Without going into details, at the moment I am simulating from a
> >> > Gaussian
> >> >  random field
> >> > , a la geostatistics, and estimating using ICAR relying on the link
> >> > between
> >> > GRFs and GMRFs.
> >> >
> >> > Karim

> >
> > as far as I understand, control.predictor(A=A) does not help!
>
> yes! using this trick.
>
> 1. make the linear predictor equals each one of the component of the
> model. so eta[1] = intercept, eta[2] = x1[1], eta[3] = x1[2], etc..,
>
> 2. build the model using the A-matrix.
>
> here is your example; I think I got it correct.
>
> ******************
>
> n = 3
> m = 6
> x1 = rnorm(m,mean=0,sd=1)
> x2 = rnorm(n,mean=0,sd=1)
> A = matrix(c(rep(1,6),c(1,0,1,0,1,0),c(0,1,0,1,0,1)),nrow=m,ncol=n)
> y = 1+x1+A%*%x2
>
>
> N = n + m + 1
> intercept = c(1, rep(NA, N-1))
> xx1 = c(NA, 1:m, rep(NA, N-(m+1)))
> xx2 = c(NA, rep(NA, m), 1:n)
>
> formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(xx1, model="iid") + f(xx2, model="iid")
> AA = matrix(0, m, N)
>
> AA[, 1] = 1
> for(i in 1:m) {
>     AA[i, 1+i] = 1
> }
>
> for(i in 1:n) {
>     AA[, N-n+i] = A[, i]
> }
>
> r = inla(formula, data = list(y=y, xx1=xx1, xx2=xx2),
>         control.predictor = list(A=AA))
>
>
